positions/lds-godhead/name: Latter-day Saint Godhead (outside historic Nicene orthodoxy)
positions/lds-godhead/oneLine: The Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost are three distinct beings, one in purpose; the Father and the Son have glorified bodies of flesh and bone.
positions/lds-godhead/coreClaims/0: Father, Son and Holy Ghost are three separate personages united in will, purpose and love.
positions/lds-godhead/coreClaims/1: God the Father is an exalted, embodied being; the Holy Ghost is a personage of spirit.
positions/lds-godhead/coreClaims/2: The Nicene doctrine of one substance is part of a ‘Great Apostasy’ corrected by restoration through Joseph Smith.
positions/lds-godhead/coreClaims/3: Humans are spirit children of heavenly parents with potential for exaltation.
positions/lds-godhead/origin: Joseph Smith's First Vision (accounts from 1832–1842) and later teachings, especially the King Follett discourse (1844) and Doctrine and Covenants 130 (1843).
positions/lds-godhead/strongestArguments: At Jesus' baptism and in Stephen's vision the Father and Son appear as distinct beings.
Jesus' prayer that his disciples be ‘one, as we are one’ (John 17:21) suggests unity of purpose, not of substance.
Latter-day Saints present it as a restoration of biblical, pre-Hellenistic belief, confirmed by modern revelation.
positions/lds-godhead/strongestObjection: Historic Christian bodies regard three distinct gods as incompatible with biblical monotheism (Isaiah 43:10; 44:6).
Divine embodiment contradicts John 4:24 (‘God is a Spirit’) and the classical doctrine of God's infinity.
The restoration claim depends on modern revelation that other Christians do not accept.
positions/lds-godhead/responses/0: LDS writers argue that ‘one God’ in Scripture refers to a united Godhead, and that early Jewish and Christian thought was more anthropomorphic than later creeds.
positions/lds-godhead/consequences/0: A key reason most Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant bodies do not recognise LDS baptism (e.g. Catholic Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, 2001).
positions/lds-godhead/consequences/1: Underlies ongoing interfaith dialogue between LDS and evangelical scholars since the 1990s.
positions/open-theism/oneLine: God is a loving, relational being who genuinely responds to creatures; because creatures are truly free, the future is partly open and God knows it as possibilities, not settled facts.
positions/open-theism/coreClaims/0: Love is God's chief attribute; God seeks real, reciprocal relationship with free creatures.
positions/open-theism/coreClaims/1: Libertarian free will means future free choices do not yet exist to be known; God knows all that is knowable.
positions/open-theism/coreClaims/2: God can change his mind, be grieved, take risks and be surprised, as Scripture says (Genesis 6:6; Jeremiah 3:7; Jonah 3:10).
positions/open-theism/coreClaims/3: God remains omnipotent and sovereign and will certainly achieve his ultimate purposes.
positions/open-theism/coreClaims/4: Classical immutability and impassibility owe more to Greek philosophy than to the Bible.
positions/open-theism/origin: Antecedents in Calcidius and some 19th-century Methodists (Lorenzo McCabe); crystallised in evangelical theology with Richard Rice (The Openness of God, 1980) and the multi-author The Openness of God (1994); debated sharply in the Evangelical Theological Society (2001–2003), which declined to expel Clark Pinnock and John Sanders.
positions/open-theism/proponentsOther/5: Thomas Jay Oord (open and relational, nearer process)
positions/open-theism/strongestArguments: It reads straightforwardly the many biblical passages in which God repents, tests, asks questions and changes course.
It offers a strong theodicy: God is not the author of evil, because he did not eternally ordain particular evils.
It makes petitionary prayer genuinely effective.
It aims to free Christian theology from Hellenistic assumptions while staying evangelical on Scripture and creation.
positions/open-theism/strongestObjection: Biblical prophecies of free human acts (Peter's denial, Judas, Cyrus named in Isaiah 44:28) seem to require exhaustive foreknowledge.
Isaiah 46:9–10 presents God's knowledge of ‘the end from the beginning’ as proof of his deity.
Classical theists argue that a God who learns and risks cannot guarantee his promises or the final victory of good.
It treats anthropomorphic texts literally but not others (God's ‘arm’, ‘eyes’), applying an inconsistent hermeneutic.
positions/open-theism/responses/0: Open theists answer that God can predict or bring about specific events without foreknowing every free act.
positions/open-theism/responses/1: They distinguish God's immutable character from his mutable experience and plans.
positions/open-theism/responses/2: They argue that the classical reading equally selects some texts (Malachi 3:6) as controlling over others.
positions/open-theism/consequences/0: Divided North American evangelical institutions in the 1990s–2000s (ETS debates; the Baptist General Conference controversy over Gregory Boyd).
positions/open-theism/consequences/1: Fuelled renewed defence of classical theism and of Arminian ‘simple foreknowledge’ and Molinist alternatives.
positions/open-theism/consequences/2: Connected with ‘relational theology’ movements in Wesleyan and Pentecostal circles.
positions/process-theology/oneLine: Reality is a creative process of events, and God is its supreme instance: dipolar (with an eternal ‘primordial’ and an ever-growing ‘consequent’ nature), luring the world by persuasive love rather than coercive power.
positions/process-theology/coreClaims/0: Becoming, not static being, is fundamental; God too is in process.
positions/process-theology/coreClaims/1: God has a primordial nature (eternal possibilities) and a consequent nature (God's experience of the world, which grows).
positions/process-theology/coreClaims/2: God acts by persuasion, offering each moment its best possibility (the ‘initial aim’), never by unilateral coercion.
positions/process-theology/coreClaims/3: God is genuinely affected by the world's joys and sufferings — ‘the fellow-sufferer who understands’ (Whitehead).
positions/process-theology/coreClaims/4: God includes the world without being identical to it (panentheism); creation ex nihilo is usually rejected.
positions/process-theology/origin: From Alfred North Whitehead's metaphysics (Process and Reality, 1929) and Charles Hartshorne's neoclassical theism (Man's Vision of God, 1941); developed theologically by John B. Cobb Jr., Schubert Ogden, Norman Pittenger, Marjorie Suchocki and David Ray Griffin, centred on Claremont, California.
positions/process-theology/strongestArgu: It offers a direct answer to the problem of evil: God does not prevent evil because God does not exercise coercive omnipotence.
It integrates theology with evolutionary science and a dynamic view of nature.
It takes seriously the biblical God who suffers with his people and whose love is vulnerable.
It has been fruitful for ecological theology and for interreligious dialogue (especially with Buddhism).
positions/process-theology/strongestObje: It abandons creation ex nihilo and God's omnipotence, which most Christians regard as essential.
It offers no assurance that good will finally triumph or of bodily resurrection.
Its God is ‘the great companion’ but arguably not the Lord worthy of worship.
Its Trinitarian theology is thin or reinterpretive; many process thinkers do not affirm a Nicene Trinity.
positions/process-theology/responses/0: Process theologians answer that persuasive love is a higher form of power than coercion, and that omnipotence as usually defined makes God responsible for evil.
positions/process-theology/responses/1: They argue that objective immortality — every event preserved in God's memory — gives the world everlasting significance.
positions/process-theology/responses/2: Some (e.g. Joseph Bracken) have developed process-Trinitarian models.
positions/process-theology/consequences/: Influential in mainline Protestant seminaries in North America (1960s–1990s) and in ecological theology.
Provoked responses from classical theists and indirectly influenced open theism, which shares its relational emphasis while retaining creation ex nihilo.
positions/byzantine-divine-liturgy/name: Byzantine Divine Liturgy (Eastern Orthodox liturgical worship)
positions/byzantine-divine-liturgy/altNa: Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom
positions/byzantine-divine-liturgy/oneLi: The Church’s worship is a participation in the heavenly liturgy: the received Divine Liturgy, with its chant, icons, incense and fixed prayers, is the primary expression and school of Orthodox faith.
positions/byzantine-divine-liturgy/coreC: In the Eucharist the Church ascends to the Kingdom and joins the angels’ worship ("Let us who mystically represent the Cherubim").
Lex orandi, lex credendi: liturgy is a source and norm of doctrine.
Received liturgical tradition is not to be altered at will; it unites the Church across time and space.
Liturgy engages the whole person: icons, incense, chant, bodily prostrations, fasting and the cycle of feasts.
Vernacular celebration has been the missionary norm (Slavonic, Arabic, Georgian, Romanian, Alaskan languages, English).
positions/byzantine-divine-liturgy/keyTe: Divine Liturgies of St John Chrysostom and St Basil
Germanus of Constantinople, Ecclesiastical History and Mystical Contemplation (8th c.)
positions/byzantine-divine-liturgy/origi: Grew from the rite of Constantinople, combining the anaphoras attributed to Basil (4th c.) and John Chrysostom (c.400) with Palestinian monastic offices (Typikon of St Sabbas); standardised between the 9th and 14th centuries and later printed (1526 onward).
positions/byzantine-divine-liturgy/stron: Revelation 4–5 portrays worship as heavenly, ordered and sung, not improvised.
Continuity of the same liturgy for over a millennium unites believers across nations and centuries.
The liturgy teaches the faith to illiterate and literate alike through the senses, and has sustained Orthodoxy under Ottoman and Soviet rule.
Protestants argue that much of it (veneration of icons, prayers to saints, sacrificial language) lacks scriptural warrant.
Length and archaic language can make participation passive for many worshippers, a concern raised by Orthodox reformers themselves.
Fixed forms can become formalism without inward faith (Isa 29:13).
positions/byzantine-divine-liturgy/respo: Orthodox reply that the liturgy is saturated with Scripture and that tradition is Scripture’s living interpretation.
They point to the active role of the people in responses, singing and communion, and to translation into vernaculars as an Orthodox missionary norm.
positions/byzantine-divine-liturgy/conse: Central identity marker of Orthodox peoples, from Greece to Russia, Georgia and Alaska.
Inspired the Western Liturgical Movement and ecumenical eucharistic theology.
Disputes over calendar and liturgical reform (e.g. Old Believer schism, 1666; Old Calendarists, 1924).
positions/oriental-and-syriac-liturgies/: Oriental Orthodox and East Syriac liturgical traditions
Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara rites
Liturgy of Addai and Mari

The ancient non-Byzantine churches of Egypt, Ethiopia, Syria, Armenia, India and Mesopotamia keep their own apostolic liturgies, languages and music, which they regard as faithful bearers of early Christian worship.
The Coptic Church celebrates the liturgies of St Basil, St Gregory and St Cyril in Coptic and Arabic.
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church uses many anaphoras in Geʿez, with Yared’s zema chant, drums, sistra and liturgical dance, and keeps a replica of the Ark (tabot) on every altar.
The Syriac Orthodox and Malankara churches use the Liturgy of St James in Syriac and Malayalam; Armenians celebrate the Badarak.
The Church of the East’s Anaphora of Addai and Mari, among the oldest in use, lacks an explicit institution narrative yet was recognised as valid by Rome (2001).
Long fasts, all-night vigils and the church year structure the life of the people.

Rooted in the rites of Alexandria, Jerusalem, Antioch and Edessa before the divisions of 431 and 451; developed in Coptic, Geʿez, Syriac and Armenian from the 4th–7th centuries (Yared in 6th-century Aksum; Mesrop Mashtots’ Armenian alphabet, 405).

Narsai of Nisibis
Catholicos Timothy I
These liturgies preserve forms and languages (Syriac is close to Jesus’ Aramaic) of the earliest centuries.
Their survival through persecution and minority status testifies to the sustaining power of liturgical tradition.
They show that apostolic worship was never uniform but diverse across cultures, a model for inculturation.
Chalcedonian churches historically judged their Christology defective; Western Protestants share the general objections to fixed liturgy and saints’ veneration.
Use of ancient languages few understand (Geʿez, Coptic, classical Syriac) can hinder participation.
Some practices (e.g. Ethiopian Old Testament food and purity customs) are criticised as Judaizing.
Since the 1980s–90s Christological agreements with Rome and the Eastern Orthodox have acknowledged a common faith in different terms.
These churches increasingly use Arabic, Amharic, Malayalam, English and other vernaculars alongside the classical languages.
Liturgy as the core of identity for Copts, Ethiopians, Armenians, Assyrians and Indian Christians under Muslim and Hindu majorities.
Diaspora communities now worship in these rites across Europe, North America and Australia.
Scholarly interest in Syriac and Ethiopian liturgy has reshaped histories of early worship.
